title: A stranger or a traveler
hookLine: be in the world as a stranger or a traveler
tomorrow: you want something badly. is the wanting itself the problem?

lines: A GATE AT SIX IN THE MORNING.
cards: An airport gate at six in the morning. One bag each, coffee in hand, nobody hanging pictures on the wall. Everyone's somewhere, and nobody's home.
Yesterday's question: what if you lived like you were only passing through? Hadith forty, in Sahih al-Bukhari, comes with a touch.
Ibn Umar says the Prophet, peace be upon him, took hold of his shoulder and said: be in the world as if you were a stranger, or a traveler on the road.

teach.h: A STRANGER: LIVES THERE, REMEMBERS HOME.
teach.b: Two pictures, and the second is lighter than the first. A stranger lives in a town that isn't his: he works there, eats there, makes friends there, but he doesn't forget where home is.
A traveler on the road doesn't even unpack; he rests and keeps moving. Notice what the hadith doesn't say. It doesn't say don't love anything, or don't build.
The stranger still lives fully. He just holds it the way you hold a borrowed room.

Then Ibn Umar, who heard it, used to add his own lines: in the evening, don't wait for the morning; in the morning, don't wait for the evening. Take from your health for your sickness, and from your life for your death.
That's the detail to tell a friend tonight: the Prophet's teaching came with a hand on the shoulder, and the student kept repeating it.
So what does it give you this week, when something big is changing, a move, a new job, a goodbye?
Permission to love where you are without gripping it.
Carry what matters. Hold the rest lightly.

how: Muslims quote this hadith, and Ibn Umar's lines after it, when speaking of not clinging to the world; teachers use it to encourage doing good now instead of waiting.

games.q: what does “a stranger or a traveler” mean?
o: a pilgrim on the road to Mecca for hajj
a refugee asking for shelter in a new land
living fully, but holding the world lightly

p: where the Prophet held Ibn Umar

s: the hadith says don't love anyone or anywhere
the stranger still works, eats and makes friends; he just remembers it isn't home.
the Prophet took Ibn Umar by the shoulder when he said it
Ibn Umar added: take from your health for your sickness
and from your life for your death.

games.q: a friend's family moves again, and she won't unpack or make friends 'since we'll leave anyway.' what does hadith forty offer her?
o: she's right: a traveler shouldn't get attached to anyone.
the stranger still lives and loves where he is; he just remembers it isn't forever.
unpack everything and treat this town as forever.
games.why: the stranger in the hadith lives fully in a town that isn't home. passing through isn't the same as refusing to arrive.

practice: Empty your pockets onto the table: keys, phone, whatever you carry. Walk slowly for about a minute, around the room or down a hall, hands empty, noticing how light you are.
Then sit for the rest of the time with your hands open in your lap, still carrying nothing.

wordCard.voice: A stranger or a traveler: two ways to live in the world without mistaking it for home. The stranger remembers; the traveler keeps moving.

orig.s: كُنْ فِي الدُّنْيَا كَأَنَّكَ غَرِيبٌ أَوْ عَابِرُ سَبِيلٍ
orig.say: kun fid-DUN-ya ka-AN-na-ka gha-REE-bun aw AA-bi-ru sa-BEEL
orig.note: Arabic: be in the world as if you were a stranger or one crossing a road. gharib, stranger.

carryVoice: For the road: just passing through, so love it, and hold it lightly. That's hadith forty.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 6416 (Ibn Umar: the Prophet took my shoulder; be in the world as a stranger or a traveler; Ibn Umar's sayings after it)
